description:
AnyDesk installed-service state. Keyvalue '=' separator. The jackpot key is ad.anynet.pkey, the DEVICE RSA PRIVATE KEY stored as a PEM block with literal \\n line-escapes. Pair with ad.anynet.id from system.conf to impersonate the victim's AnyDesk device on the anynet without ever triggering unattended-access prompts.
ad.license.state_store is the signed license binding (hex blob); useful for license fraud correlation across victims.

AnyDesk machine-wide config. Keyvalue '=' separator. Carries the AnyDesk ID (ad.anynet.id, the stable 10-digit anynet device address), the license name + cache hash, the alias (anynet dns-like handle), and the frontend clipboard permission flags. Pair with the service private key from service.conf for silent device takeover.

Opus / vowel-stripped autofill dumps under Browsers/AtFs/*.txt. Name/Value blocks separated by '===============' divider. Captures what's likely KYC-grade PII for the victim (seen with CPF / CEP / DataNascimento / DataEmissaoIdentidade / CPFRepresentante in the Brazilian victim 6627).

Opus / vowel-stripped browser bookmarks under Browsers/Bmas/*.txt. Flat URL list, one bookmark per line. Captures operator-interest signal: which banks, exchanges, admin panels, internal corp URLs the victim had saved. Regex pulls one URL per record; bulkParse returns one record per bookmark.

Android app credentials: `android://<hash>@<com.pkg.name>/<delim>user<delim>pass` where delim is pipe or colon. ulpextract runs this BEFORE the generic scheme strip so the hash@pkg doesn't get misread as a URL path. We give it the highest combolist priority (30) for the same reason. The hash can be any length when scheme is literal 'android://'; other schemes would need a stricter hash length check to avoid false positives.

Catches any-scheme ULPs beyond http(s): ftp://, smb://, chrome-extension://, app://, and the long tail of proprietary schemes stealer logs include. Mirrors ulpextract.leadingSchm (`[a-z][a-z0-9+-]*://`). Pipe is the cleanest field separator for this shape (ssh paths and chrome-extension IDs frequently contain colons).

Fallback container that matches ANY drop. Priority 1 so every real stealer-family container (priority 100) wins before this fires. Once the four known families above have been exhausted, we tag the drop "combolist" so the per-file probe rules can classify its line shape. min_score 0 + empty requires = unconditional match.

Email-anchored combos with no URL: user@domain:password. Priority 25 (above the ULP probes at 10-20) so a line that parses as email-only isn't misclassified as a ULP with a weird host. Mirrors the leadingEmail path in ulpextract.parseLine.

Schemeless host combos: example.com/path:user:pass (no http:// prefix). Mirrors ulpextract.leadingURL which accepts IPv4 or dotted-host anchors. Lower priority (12) than scheme-anchored rules so an http:// line still matches the stricter probe first.

"URL:user:pass" ULP shape. Harder than the semicolon / pipe variants because URLs contain colons (scheme, port). The regex anchors on https?://, then consumes the URL up to the LAST colon before a non-URL-looking tail. Priority 10 so the clean separators probe first. Known false-negative: user or password containing a colon. ulpextract is still the ground truth for bulk parsing.
"URL|user|pass" ULP shape. Pipe is clean (URLs don't contain it). Common in forum dumps that use `|` to avoid both the `:` URL-port collision and the `;` CRLF-render quirk some tools have.
Probe for the "URL;user;pass" ULP shape. Semicolon is the clean separator because URLs do not contain it. One sample row enough to confirm shape; ulpextract remains the per-row credential ingester.

ulpextract's OWN output format: host<TAB>url<TAB>login<TAB>password per line. We parse our pipeline's downstream artefact so operators can round-trip normalized log files through the workbench without re-running the extractor.

Windows Credential Manager export (DPAPI-unwrapped). Blocks are Target / User / Pass separated by blank lines. Pass may be either a plaintext password OR a long base64/JWT token (OAuth refresh, Xbox Live auth, OneDrive, etc.); operator should treat anything in the Pass field as sensitive regardless of apparent shape. User is often 'N/A' when the credential is a bearer token with no explicit user.

Sidecar presence probe for an Exodus wallet in the victim folder. Priority 40 (below the primary stealer-family containers at 100+) so json_v2 / lumma / redline / stealc still win the family verdict; this rule shows up in the trace as a matched sidecar so an analyst knows the victim has Exodus installed. The seed.seco binary IS encrypted but having it + a weak passphrase = funds-at-risk.

FileZilla Site Manager export. One record per <Server> under <FileZilla3><Servers>. Port is cast to int; password stays raw base64 (FileZilla's 'encoding' attribute is informational, the obfuscation is just b64) so the pipeline can decode after insert. The engine uses a hardened in-tree XML parser: no DOCTYPE, no external entity resolution, only the five standard XML entities, depth cap 256, zero network reachability (no fetch code path exists in the parser).

Firefox logins.json pivoted on $.logins: one record per saved login. encryptedUsername / encryptedPassword are base64-wrapped PKCS#7 blobs that need key4.db + the master password (empty by default) to decrypt. Even before decryption, the per-login hostname list is CTI-grade inventory (bank domains vs forum domains = very different triage priority).

Sidecar probe: tags a drop as carrying the Gabb file-grabber component. Priority 50, lower than the real family containers (100+), so the containing family (json_v2 etc.) still wins the family verdict; this rule shows up as a matched entry in the trace so an analyst sees the grabber is present without having to eyeball the folder listing. requires: Gabb/ dir + at least one of the four known profile buckets.

JSON-first family cluster: StealC v2, Acreed, Stealerium. All three emit pc_info.json + log_info.json; single-folder disambiguation is not reliable without BuildID prefix or C2 telemetry. Catalog them as one logical family "json_v2" and let a downstream classifier sub-tag by log_info.BuildID (dedicated rule, to be added).

Exfil manifest metadata. Priority 110 (above pc_info at 100) so counts + CreatedOnUtc override anything of the same name from pc_info. BuildID observed in some sub-variants but NOT in Khazan intake (2026-11), so required key is now CreatedOnUtc which is universal across StealC v2 / Acreed / Stealerium builds seen so far. IsHaveGrabberFiles is the signal that the drop ships the Gabb file-grabber sidecar: integer > 0 = present, 0 = absent.

Victim metadata from StealC-v2 / Acreed / Stealerium pc_info.json. Top level is a flat object; GPU and LocalAdapterIpList are arrays, which flow through JSONPath-lite as JSON-stringified blobs (good for raw retention, searchable downstream). LocalTime is "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" without a timezone: we parse it iso8601 (Python's fromisoformat + JS's Date.parse both accept the space separator).

Lumma victim-folder predicate. Clean match: System.txt present AND at least two of the native Lumma sidecar files are there. Rejects Raccoon (which can also ship System.txt) via the min_score; a bare System.txt without sidecars falls through to raccoon_container.

Lumma victim header. Native shape is "- Key: Value" (dash prefix, then colon-space). We key the extract map by the literal "- Key" so the dash is part of the lookup; case-insensitive match handles the rare all-caps/lowercased variants. HWID uniqueness (UUID-style) is the Lumma-vs-Raccoon tiebreak downstream; we extract it as-is here.

Netscape cookie file format. Tab-separated, 7 columns: domain, include_subdomains (TRUE/FALSE), path, secure (TRUE/FALSE), expires (unix epoch), name, value. Lines starting with '#' are comments; blank lines are skipped. Glob `**ookies**` catches both `Cookies*` and `cookies*` variants at any depth via the common `ookies` substring (our glob treats `**` as `.*`, so bookending it around a substring makes the pattern cross path separators); stealer families emit this file under Browsers/, Cookies/, or similar sibling dirs. One sample row extracted as a probe (DELIMITER matcher is first-row-only by design); bulk cookie ingest is a pipeline-side job.

Opus (WEB RAT) victim-folder predicate, v2 (predicate-tree form). Catches BOTH:

  (a) classic Opus: UserInformation.txt AND worklog.txt (even if the
      sidecar dirs are thin)
  (b) Opus-missing-worklog: UserInformation.txt AND at least 3 of the
      Opus-specific sidecars (Clients/<messenger> OR Telegram/ /
      Extensions/ / Wallets/ / Files/). An operator may ship with
      worklog disabled; the sidecar density still identifies it as
      Opus, not RedLine.

Mutual-exclusion arm rejects any drop that also carries the json_v2 / Lumma / StealC signatures (pc_info.json / System.txt / information.txt) so disambiguation is one-sided.
Priority 110 beats redline_container (100) on the UserInformation.txt collision when either arm of the top-level OR fires.

Opus (WEB RAT) system/user recon file. Filename collides with RedLine's but the container-family gate ensures this rule only fires inside an Opus drop. Opus's Rust stub bundles screen + userinfo in a single file; starting shape is a conservative keyvalue map against the fields the operator says they see consistently. Refine from the operator's API docs when ready; this rule is intentionally wide so unseen keys survive as ignored, not break the pipeline.

RedLine Passwords.txt block shape. Keys: URL, Username, Password. Blocks separated by 15 '=' chars on their own line. No Soft/SOFT field (RedLine stores the browser elsewhere). Fires alongside the two block-shape rules; only one anchors in any given file.

Title-case passwords.txt block format. 402 of 439 Khazan victims ship this shape (dominant). Blocks separated by blank lines. Keys: Soft, Host, Login, Password. Host may contain either https:// URLs OR android://<hash>@<pkg>/ app references. REGEX matcher is single-shot per call; bulkParse iterates every block when the Workbench asks for all records.

UPPERCASE passwords.txt block format. 37 of 439 Khazan victims ship this (json_v2 cluster: StealC v2 / Acreed / Stealerium). Often BOM-prefixed. Keys: SOFT, URL, USER, PASS. Fires in parallel with passwords_block_title; whichever shape matches a given file wins because the other regex simply won't find its anchor.

Per-victim TSV credentials file shipped by the json_v2 cluster (StealC v2 / Acreed / Stealerium). Tab-separated `url \t username \t password` per line. This rule only captures the FIRST row as a sample (the DELIMITER matcher is single-row by design); the pipeline's ulpextract pass remains the authoritative credential ingester for the full file. Here it serves as a sanity probe that the archive is well-formed before a victim dossier is committed.

RedLine victim-folder predicate, v2 (predicate-tree form). Explicit Opus / json_v2 / Lumma / StealC exclusions so a drop that LOOKS like RedLine but actually isn't gets correctly rejected. Requires at least two of the three RedLine-specific sidecar signals (Browsers/ dir with per-browser Passwords layout, InstalledSoftware.txt, Screenshot.jpg).
Opus-exclusion arm: a UserInformation.txt drop that ALSO carries worklog.txt OR a Clients/<messenger> file is NOT RedLine, no matter how many other sidecars match. Previously this rule required only the filename and the min_score; now it says so explicitly.

RedLine header. Covers TWO shape variants seen in the wild:

  textbook  (short keys):  Computer / User / OS / CPU / RAM
  newer     (long keys):   Computer Name / User Name /
                           Operation System / Installed RAM / Processor
                           (plus Traffic / Log date / Version Build /
                           Admin Group / Integrity / TimeZone)

requires_keys gates on HWID alone (present in both). Both extract maps write to the SAME output fields where they overlap (hostname/user/os/ cpu/ram/language), so a rule change doesn't fragment downstream schemas. Only one of the two key styles is typically present per file, so the overlapping extracts don't collide.

Riot Client session cookies. Three cookies grant full RSO (Riot Sign On) access, bypassing password + 2FA across every Riot title (League / Valorant / TFT / LoR / Wild Rift): tdid, ssid, csid. Each stored under rso-authenticator.<name> as a cookie object with value / expiryTime / domain / path.

StealC v1 victim-folder predicate. information.txt is the hinge; Autofill/ + Cookies/ + History/ tree confirms it. Vidar ships the same file name under repack, so a bare information.txt without the grabber dirs falls through to a lower-priority Vidar probe later.

StealC v1 information.txt pre-section header. Plain "Key: Value" lines BEFORE the [Hardware] / [Software] INI sections. A second rule (stealc_information_sections, priority 100) handles the INI body; the two rules extract disjoint field sets and merge.

StealC v1 [Hardware] section extraction. The [Software] section is a bare program list (no `=` separator), so we don't try to parse it here; a dedicated software-inventory rule can lift it later via delimiter type if that signal becomes useful.

Steam's loginusers.vdf: one record per SteamID the victim has signed into on this machine. $key resolves to the SteamID64; the remaining fields come from the per-account VDF subtree. RememberPassword=1 + captured ssfn* session files = silent session takeover.
Glob matches both the vanilla 'loginusers.vdf' and 'Loginusers.vdf', under Software/Stam/ (json_v2 sidecar), Steam/config/ (direct grab), or wherever the stealer flattened it.

Sidecar presence probe for Steam ssfn* session files. Pair with a loginusers.vdf entry where RememberPassword=1 for silent session takeover (no account password / Steam Guard prompt). Priority 40 so the primary stealer family still wins; this just surfaces the session-material inventory.

Sidecar presence probe for Telegram Desktop tdata/ session dir. Priority 40 so the primary stealer family wins; this surfaces in the trace so an analyst immediately sees 'this drop has a Telegram session'. The D877F783D5D3EF8C file is the primary tdata session blob; its presence alone (no decryption needed) is the signal.
